# Forced supporting contacts and exact global-cut compression

This note proves a continuous supporting-slope selection with exactly the
contacts forced by actual anchored inclusions. It strengthens finite
averaging of projected slopes to ONE bounded continuous feasible slope
with the exact forced contact set. The resulting global convex cuts are
actual deformations. Removing extra contacts minimizes their nonnegative
costs, but does not automatically improve signed cap payments.

Throughout `d>=1`, use the finite positive compatible family and canonical
fiber hull of
`candidate 6748c967393345b9`.
That source supplies the actual global cuts and their proved nonsmooth
first variations. No polyhedral fiber assumption is made.

## 1. The feasible slopes and the forced-contact definition

Fix a source base `p` and write, for unit continuous normal `u`,

    v_z=z-p,  c_z(u)=h_z(u)-h_p(u),
    F_u={A in R^n:v_z.A>=c_z(u) for all z in P}.         (1)

These nonempty closed polyhedra have a FIXED constraint matrix. Their
feasibility follows from actual anchored Minkowski inclusions and finite
Farkas, as proved in the cited source. Define the nonnegative slack

    Delta_z(A,u)=v_z.A-c_z(u).

Call `z` forced at `u` if `Delta_z(A,u)=0` for EVERY `A in F_u`.
The source base itself is always forced. No arbitrary selected supporting
plane is used in this definition.

## 2. Projections onto the feasible slope polyhedron vary continuously

For a fixed vector `q`, let `P_q(u)` be its Euclidean projection onto
`F_u`. This is continuous and bounded as a function of `u`.

Here is a direct proof valid with lower-dimensional feasible polyhedra
and deficient base rank. Projection optimality gives

    P_q-q=V_I^T lambda_I,  lambda_I>=0,

using active constraint rows. A minimal conic representation uses
independent rows; redundant rows can be removed by moving coefficients
along a dependence until one vanishes. For this independent row set,

    P_q=q+V_I^T(V_I V_I^T)^(-1)[c_I-V_I q].              (2)

The empty row set covers `P_q=q`. There are finitely many such formulas.
For convergent feasible right-hand sides, their projections are bounded
by (2). On a subsequence with the same row set, feasibility, active
equalities, and nonnegative multipliers all pass to the limit. The
limiting KKT condition identifies the unique projection for the limiting
right-hand side. This proves continuity without a Slater assumption.
Compactness of the normal sphere gives boundedness for each fixed `q`.

Also, projection nonexpansiveness at a fixed `u` gives the useful uniform
growth estimate

    |P_q(u)|<=|q|+M_0,
    M_0=max_u |P_0(u)|<infinity.                         (3)

The usual projection variational inequalities at `q` and `0`, added
together, give `|P_q-P_0|^2<=(P_q-P_0).q`, proving this bound directly.

## 3. Finite contact compression and an exact continuous selection

Choose a countable dense sequence `q_0,q_1,...` in `R^n`, with `q_0=0`.
For `n=0`, use the repeated unique vector. Define finite averages

    A_m(u)=(1/(m+1)) sum_(j=0)^m P_(q_j)(u).             (4)

Each is bounded, continuous, and feasible. Since all slacks are
nonnegative, its contact set at every `u` is exactly

    {z:Delta_z(A_m,u)=0}
      =intersection_(j=0)^m {z:Delta_z(P_(q_j),u)=0}.    (5)

These sets decrease with `m`. Their intersection is the forced set.
Indeed, if `A in F_u` gives a positive slack at `z`, choose a sequence
of dense targets approaching `A`. Nonexpansiveness and `P_A=A` show
that their projections approach `A`, and one therefore has positive
slack at `z`. This argument is pointwise for EVERY normal, not merely
almost every normal.

There is no need to let the actual body tend to a limit. In fact a
single exact selection exists. Put

    alpha_j=2^(-j-1)/(1+|q_j|),
    omega_j=alpha_j/(sum_l alpha_l)>0,
    A_*(u)=sum_(j=0)^infinity omega_j P_(q_j)(u).        (6)

The weights sum to one and `sum omega_j |q_j|<infinity`. By (3), this
series converges uniformly on the normal sphere. Thus `A_*` is bounded
and continuous. Its partial normalized convex combinations are feasible,
so their limit is feasible as well. Linearity of the constraints gives

    Delta_z(A_*,u)=sum_j omega_j Delta_z(P_(q_j),u).

Every term is nonnegative and every weight positive. Equations (5)--(6)
therefore prove the exact identity

    Delta_z(A_*(u),u)=0
       iff z is forced at u.                           (7)

This is simultaneous for all bases and all normals. It can equivalently
be described as choosing a relative-interior point of each feasible
slope polyhedron, but (6) proves the needed continuity explicitly.

## 4. Exact algebraic meaning: tight anchored representations

Let

    Lambda_p={lambda>=0:sum_z lambda_z=1,
                          sum_z lambda_z z=p}.

Then `z` is forced at `u` if and only if there is a representation
`lambda in Lambda_p` such that

    lambda_z>0,
    h_p(u)=sum_w lambda_w h_w(u).                       (8)

For the reverse implication, average the nonnegative slacks against
`lambda`. Their sum is zero by (8), so every positively weighted slack
vanishes for every feasible slope.

For the forward implication with a nonsource constraint, maximize
`v_z.A` over the nonempty polyhedron `VA>=c`. Forced equality means its
finite optimum is `c_z`. Finite linear-programming duality supplies
`t>=0` with

    sum_w t_w v_w=-v_z,
    sum_w t_w c_w=-c_z.

Adding the unit coefficient at `z` produces nonnegative coefficients
with zero base moment and zero total support difference. Normalize their
positive sum to obtain (8), retaining a positive coefficient at `z`.
For `z=p`, the trivial self representation proves the assertion.

Equivalently, one may require in (8) an EXTREME representation. Decompose
`lambda` into vertices of the finite polytope `Lambda_p`. Every actual
support gap `h_p-sum lambda_w h_w` is nonnegative; a zero weighted average
forces every used extreme gap to be zero, and at least one used extreme
representation retains positive weight at `z`.

Consequently, for a fixed `z`, the forced normal set is the finite union
of the closed sets

    {u:h_p(u)-sum_w lambda_w^e h_w(u)=0}

over extreme anchored representations with `lambda_z^e>0`. It is closed
and measurable. Geometrically, a tight relation gives the actual face
inclusion

    sum_w lambda_w F_(K_w)(u) subset F_(K_p)(u).

It asserts directional support equality. It does not assert equality
of the full Minkowski bodies, disjoint contact cells, or a drop in
contact dimension.

## 5. Actual first variations with forced contacts only

Keep all source projective fields and affine base denominator parameters
FIXED while selecting slopes. In the notation of the global-cut source,
these are the continuous globally convex fields

    Phi_(i,z)(u,x)=H_i(u)
       f_i(1+a_i.(x-y_i)+b_i(u).(z-p_i)).

For each of finitely many sources choose the slope (6), and intersect
the original canonical hull with all the corresponding global convex
cuts. This is one actual compatible nested family for small positive
erosion parameter. Positivity of all original integer fibers, the
projection, and the deficient-rank repair are exactly as in the cited
construction.

At a regular boundary point of `K_z`, with outward unit normal `u_z(x)`,
its exact first normal speed is

    v_z^*(x)=max({Phi_(i,z)(u_z(x),x):
                    z forced for source p_i at u_z(x)} union {0}). (9)

Thus the total and any fixed closed ambient cap first losses are exactly

    D^*=sum_z int_(boundary K_z) v_z^* dS,
    D_H^*=sum_z int_(boundary K_z) kappa_(z,H) v_z^* dS. (10)

Here `kappa` is the ACTUAL inward-loss selector: whole/inside-supporting
traces use one, empty/outside-supporting traces use zero, and proper
traces use the strict interior cap indicator on the boundary. Pure
integer closed boundary fibers retain their full capture bit. These
formulas use the proved radial first-variation theorem, which permits
the contact indicator to be discontinuous. For `d=1`, its two boundary
points with counting surface measure give the same formulas directly.

Every other feasible slope selection has all forced contacts and may
have additional ones. With the same fixed fields it therefore has
pointwise speed at least (9), and total AND individual cap losses at
least (10). This is an exact minimal contact-cost statement, not an
optimality statement for the signed response `D_H-beta D`.

## 6. Finite approximations, strict margins, and limits of payment

If finite formulas are preferred, use the first `m` averages (4) at
every source. Their contact sets decrease to the forced sets, so the
corresponding speeds decrease pointwise to (9). The fields have one
fixed uniform bound on the finitely many original fiber boundaries,
independent of `m`. Dominated convergence gives

    D_m -> D^*,  D_(H,m) -> D_H^*                       (11)

for every fixed cap, simultaneously on any finite menu. Both nonnegative
loss sequences are decreasing, but their signed normalized differences
need not be monotone. No uniform bound on the finite-average slopes as
`m` grows is required.

For an actual fixed finite critical cover of raw mass `Q`, original
total mass `M`, and `beta=Q/M`, suppose every critical row satisfies

    D_H^*-beta D^*>0.                                  (12)

Then the exact selection (6) gives actual strict normalized descent by
the global-cut first-variation theorem. Alternatively, (11) allows one
to fix a FINITE `m` preserving all strict margins and only then choose
a sufficiently small erosion parameter. Other cover rows with strict
original mass slack remain harmless. There is no exchange of a limit
in slopes with a limit of bodies and no assertion that (12) always holds.

For one source, its own base is forced in every direction and its own
speed is exactly the prescribed projective speed. If every offsource
forced normal set is null for that offsource fiber's surface-area normal
measure, then `D^*` equals the prescribed own cost `D_p`. Every containing
source cap loses at least `Gamma_d D_p`, so a one-witness critical cover
with `beta<Gamma_d` strictly descends. At an exposed base there are no
nonself anchored representations, recovering this special case directly.
No assertion that an interior source satisfies this null-overlap premise
is made.

The improvement proved here is exact compression to the support contacts
required by actual anchored relations. It retains the original fiber
mass, the same fixed cap selectors, and the maximum where source demands
overlap. Neither a parity bound on the remaining cost nor a universal
paying choice of fields or critical menus is inferred.
